project.name: Showpass
project.footer: Source of truth: the SQL files in `db/migrations/`. This is a synthetic example schema that ships with the plugin; no real company's data is described here.

labels.softDeleteWhy: The row is hidden straight away (`deleted_at`). The nightly purge job removes it for good after 30 days.

badges.stored counts: A running total kept on the row so the ticket page doesn't count rows on every view. Moved by the checkout transaction, repaired nightly.
badges.soft delete: Deleting sets `deleted_at` and hides the row. Nothing is removed until the purge job runs.

attendees.purpose: One row per ticket, with the name that will be checked at the door.

columns.event_id: Copied from the order so door scanning never has to join through `orders`
columns.order_id: With `line_no`, the order line this ticket was bought on
columns.line_no: Part of the link to `order_lines`, not a number the buyer sees
columns.email: Where this ticket was sent. NULL when the buyer kept all tickets in their own name
columns.barcode: Printed on the ticket and scanned at the door. Unique across every event
columns.seat_label: Set only for `reserved` ticket types; NULL for general admission
columns.status: `transferred` means the name changed, not that the ticket moved order
columns.transferred_at: Last time the name on the ticket was changed

notes: Buying three tickets on one line creates three rows here, one per seat.
Changing the name on a ticket updates this row. The order and its totals never change.

examples.intro: An attendee row is one ticket: the name on it, the barcode the door scans, and the order line it was bought on. Buying three tickets on one line makes three rows here.

groups.name: Which ticket
groups.text: Three ids for the same ticket, each for a different reader.

id.means: The internal number, for joins only. It is never sent to a browser or the app. [[check_ins]] points at it.

public_id.means: The ticket's id outside the server, for example in the buyer's app. Random, so nobody can guess another ticket's id or count them.

barcode.means: The code printed on the ticket and scanned at the door. It is the only id the door app ever sees, and no two tickets share one, across every event.

groups.name: Where it came from
text: Every ticket was bought on an order line. A line's key is two columns, `(order_id, line_no)`, so the ticket points at it with the same two columns at once.
`event_id` is *denormalised*: copied here from the order, although it could be looked up through it, so door scanning never has to join through [[orders]].

event_id.means: The event the ticket is for, copied from the order.

order_id.means: The order the ticket was bought on. With `line_no`, it names the exact line in [[order_lines]]. Deleting that line, or the whole order, deletes the ticket too.

line_no.means: The number of that line inside the order. Part of the link to [[order_lines]], not a number the buyer sees.

ticket_type_id.means: The kind of ticket, from [[ticket_types]]. A ticket type that has tickets can't be deleted: the database refuses.

groups.name: Who it is for, and where they sit
groups.text: The name here is the one checked at the door. Changing it updates this row; the order and its totals never change.

full_name.means: The name on the ticket, when one was given.

email.means: Where this ticket was sent. NULL when the buyer kept all tickets in their own name; the buyer's address is on the order, in `buyer_email`. The door can also find tickets by event and email when someone has lost their barcode.
examples: a ticket in someone else's name
the buyer kept all tickets in their own name

seat_label.means: The seat, up to 16 characters. Set only for `reserved` ticket types; NULL for general admission.

groups.name: Where it is in its life
groups.text: A ticket starts `issued` and becomes `checked_in` at the door. `transferred` and `void` are the two other states it can be in.

status.means: What the ticket is right now.

examples.issued: Valid, and not used at the door yet. Every ticket starts here.
examples.transferred: The name on it was changed. It is still on the same order.
examples.void: Cancelled by a full refund or a fraud case. The door refuses it.
examples.checked_in: Scanned and let in at the door.

transferred_at.means: The last time the name on the ticket was changed. NULL if it never was.

created_at.means: When the ticket row was made.

records.name: A ticket in the buyer's name
records.text: One of the two General admission tickets on Amira's order 90412. She kept both in her own name, so `email` is empty. General admission has no seat.

records.name: A ticket passed to a friend
records.text: The buyer of order 90461 changed the name on this ticket to Leo's. `transferred` means only that the name changed: the ticket is still on the same order.

records.name: A reserved seat, let in
records.text: One of Priya's two reserved seats on order 88120. It has a seat label because its ticket type is `reserved`, and it has been scanned in at the door.

records.name: A void ticket
records.text: Noor's order was refunded in full, so the ticket is `void`. The row stays, and the door refuses its barcode.

scenarios.title: The ticket is scanned at the door
scenarios.text: Priya's barcode is scanned and she is let in. The scan is a row in [[check_ins]], and the ticket becomes `checked_in`.

scenarios.title: A ticket is passed on
scenarios.text: The buyer of order 90461 can't use the ticket and puts Leo's name on it. This row is updated; the order and its totals don't change.

scenarios.title: The order is refunded in full
scenarios.text: Noor's whole order is refunded. That makes the ticket `void`, and a void ticket is refused at the door.

audit_log.purpose: One row per change an organizer or admin made.

columns.actor_user_id: NULL for changes made by a background job or by support tooling
columns.entity_type: Table name, as written in the migrations
columns.entity_id: The row's `id` in `entity_type`. Deliberately not a foreign key, so the log outlives the row
columns.before: The changed columns only, not the whole row
columns.after: The changed columns only, not the whole row
columns.ip: Of the request that made the change, when there was one

notes: Append only. Nothing in the application updates or deletes a row here.

examples.intro: One row is one change made to an organization's data: who made it, which row it touched, and what the changed columns held before and after. Rows are only ever added: nothing in the application updates or deletes them.

groups.name: Who made the change
groups.text: Every entry belongs to an organization. The person behind it can be missing: a change made by a background job or by support tooling has none.

organization_id.means: The organization the change belongs to. Its activity feed lists these entries, newest first. If the organization is deleted for real, its entries go with it.

actor_user_id.means: The person who made the change, in [[users]]. NULL for a change made by a background job or by support tooling. It is also cleared if that person's account is deleted later.
examples: a background job, support tooling, or an account deleted since

ip.means: The IP address (the network address a request comes from) of the request that made the change, when there was one. It is stored as `inet`, PostgreSQL's type for IP addresses, which holds both the short IPv4 form and the longer IPv6 form.

groups.name: What was done, and to which row
groups.text: `entity_type` and `entity_id` together point at the row that changed. There is deliberately no foreign key behind them, so the log outlives the rows it describes.

action.means: What kind of change it was. The list lives in the application (`app/services/audit.rb`), not in the database: the column accepts any text, so even a typo is stored as it is.

examples.published: Something was published, such as an event.
examples.cancelled: Something was cancelled, such as an event.
examples.refunded: Money went back to a buyer.
examples.role_changed: A member's role in an organization changed.

entity_type.means: Which table the changed row is in, by the table's name as written in the migrations.

entity_id.means: The changed row's `id` in the table `entity_type` names. Not a foreign key, on purpose: when that row is deleted, the number stays here and so does the entry.

scenarios.title: The row it describes is deleted
scenarios.text: An organizer deletes the discount code SPRING10 (id 77) after its sale ends. A new entry records the delete. The older entries about code 77 keep `entity_id` 77 even though the row is gone, because there is no foreign key to clear it.

groups.name: What changed
text: Both columns are *jsonb*: JSON (a text format of names and values, like `{"price_cents": 2500}`) stored in a form PostgreSQL can search.
They hold only the columns that changed, not the whole row. The table below shows how the entry for a cancelled event reads.

before.means: The changed columns as they were before the change.

after.means: The same columns after the change.

records.name: An organizer changes a price
records.text: Ana raises a ticket type's price from 25.00 to 30.00. Only `price_cents` changed, so it is the only thing in `before` and `after`. Orders already sold keep their own copy of the price.

records.name: An organizer cancels an event
records.text: Mei cancels event 3120. `status` and `cancelled_at` change together, so both are in the entry. Her request came from an IPv6 address.

records.name: A change with no person behind it
records.text: The checkout job sets an event to `sold_out` when its last ticket type fills. No person made this change, so `actor_user_id` is empty, and so is `ip`.

scenarios.title: The person who made a change is deleted
scenarios.text: Ana's [[users]] row is removed for real. Her entries stay, with `actor_user_id` cleared. From then on they look the same as a change made by a background job or by support tooling.

scenarios.title: The organization is deleted
scenarios.text: If an organization is removed for real, every entry it has goes with it. Apart from that, rows never leave this table: nothing in the application deletes them.

check_ins.purpose: One row per scan at the door, including the scans that were turned away.

columns.checked_in_by: The door staff member. NULL once their account is deleted
columns.device_label: Whatever the scanning app calls itself, e.g. `Gate B iPad`
columns.result: Only `ok` lets someone in. The rest are kept so the door can be audited

notes: A failed scan is a row too. Counting people in means counting `result = 'ok'`.
`event_id` is denormalised from `attendees` so the door query stays on one table.

examples.intro: A check-in is one scan of a ticket at the door, whether it let someone in or not. The turned-away scans are kept too, so a disputed night can be read back.

groups.name: Which ticket, at which event
groups.text: `event_id` is *denormalised*: copied from the ticket in [[attendees]], although it could be looked up there, so the door's queries stay on this one table.

id.means: The internal number of the scan.

attendee_id.means: The ticket that was scanned, from [[attendees]]. If the ticket is deleted, its scans go with it.

event_id.means: The ticket's event, copied from [[attendees]]. The live door feed reads this table by event, newest scan first.

groups.name: What the door decided
text: Only `ok` lets someone in, so counting people in means counting the `ok` rows, not all rows. The table shows three scans at event 2990: three rows, two people in.
The database allows only one `ok` row per ticket, so the same ticket can't be let in twice, even from two gates at once.

result.means: What the scan decided. Every value except `ok` is a scan that was turned away, kept so the door can be audited.

examples.duplicate: Turned away as a repeat: this ticket was already let in.
examples.wrong_event: Turned away: the ticket is for a different event.

scanned_at.means: When the scan happened. The database fills in the current time if none is given.

checked_in_by.means: The door staff member who scanned, from [[users]]. NULL once their account is deleted; the scan stays.

device_label.means: Whatever the scanning app calls itself. It can be empty.

records.name: A ticket let in
records.text: Priya's reserved seat is scanned at Gate B and she walks in. This is the one `ok` row that ticket can ever have.

records.name: The same ticket again
records.text: Fifteen minutes later the same barcode turns up at Gate A. It is turned away, and the scan is still kept as a row.

records.name: Scanned by an account that's gone
records.text: An ordinary `ok` scan, but the staff member's account was deleted later, so `checked_in_by` is empty. The scan itself stays.

scenarios.title: Two gates scan the same ticket at once
text: One barcode is scanned at Gate A and Gate B in the same second.
The database allows only one `ok` row per ticket, so only one gate lets the person in. The other scan is turned away, and is a row too.

scenarios.title: A staff account is deleted
scenarios.text: A door staff member's account is deleted after the event. Their scans stay, with `checked_in_by` cleared, so the night's count doesn't change.

discount_codes.purpose: One row per code a buyer can type at checkout.

columns.event_id: NULL for a code that works on every event the organization sells
columns.code: Compared case-insensitively by the application; stored as typed
columns.amount_off_cents: Set only when `kind = 'amount'`, in the order's currency
columns.redemption_count: Raised inside the checkout transaction, so two buyers can't pass the limit

examples.intro: A discount code is something a buyer types at checkout to pay less. Each row says how much it takes off, on which events, how many orders may use it, and in what window.

groups.name: Which code, and where it works
groups.text: A code belongs to one organization. It can be tied to one of that organization's events, or left open for all of them.

id.means: The internal number. [[orders]] point at it through `discount_code_id`.

organization_id.means: The organization the code belongs to. The pair `(organization_id, code)` is unique: two organizations can both have a SPRING10, but one organization can't have two.

event_id.means: The one event the code works on. NULL for a code that works on every event the organization sells. Deleting that event deletes the code with it.
examples: on any of the organization's events

code.means: What the buyer types. It is stored as the organizer typed it, and the application compares it case-insensitively, so `spring10` finds `SPRING10`.

groups.name: How much it takes off
groups.text: `kind` decides which of the two amount columns is used. The database checks the pair: exactly one of them is filled, and its number has to make sense.

kind.means: Whether the code takes off a share of the price or a fixed sum.

examples.percent: A percentage off; the size is in `percent_off`.
examples.amount: A fixed amount off; the size is in `amount_off_cents`.

percent_off.means: The percentage, as a whole number from 1 to 100. Set only when `kind` is `percent`; NULL otherwise.

amount_off_cents.means: The fixed amount, in whole cents of the order's currency, so 5.00 is `500`. Set only when `kind` is `amount`, and always more than 0; NULL otherwise.

groups.name: How many times it can be used
text: A *redemption* is one order using the code. `redemption_count` is a *stored count*: a running total kept on the row, so checkout doesn't have to count orders every time.
A code with no limit, or with `redemption_count` still below `max_redemptions`, is one a checkout may still accept. The database keeps an index of just those codes.

max_redemptions.means: How many orders may use the code in total. NULL means unlimited.

redemption_count.means: How many orders have used the code so far. It is raised inside the checkout transaction, so two buyers can't pass the limit. The nightly count repair recounts it from the orders and corrects any drift.

scenarios.title: Two buyers take the last use at once
scenarios.text: CREW50 allows 20 orders and has had 19. Two buyers check out with it at the same moment. The count is raised inside each checkout transaction, so only one of them gets the code, and the count stops at the limit.

groups.name: When it can be used
groups.text: `starts_at` and `ends_at` are the code's window. Either can be left empty. When both are set, the database checks that the window ends after it starts.

starts_at.means: When the window opens, if the code has a start.

ends_at.means: When the window closes, if the code has an end. It must be later than `starts_at` when both are set.

created_by.means: The account that created the code, from [[users]]. NULL once that account is deleted; the code itself stays.

records.name: A percentage code for every event
records.text: SPRING10 takes 10% off on any event organization 12 sells, with no limit on uses, inside a set window. Amira used it on order 90412.

records.name: A fixed amount off one event
records.text: WELCOME5 takes 5.00 off, only on event 3051, for up to 200 orders. It has a start but no end, so `ends_at` is empty.

records.name: A code that is used up
records.text: CREW50 allowed 20 orders and has had 20, so it is no longer a code a checkout may still accept. The account that created it has since been deleted, so `created_by` is empty.

scenarios.title: A buyer uses the code
text: Amira types `spring10` at checkout. The application matches it to SPRING10 without caring about case.
Her order gets `discount_code_id` 77 and 500 cents off, 10% of her 5000. In the same checkout transaction, `redemption_count` goes up by one.

scenarios.title: The code is deleted
scenarios.text: The organizer deletes SPRING10. The orders that used it stay: their `discount_code_id` is cleared, and their `discount_cents` keeps the money that was taken off.

scenarios.title: The stored count drifts
scenarios.text: If `redemption_count` ever ends up different from the number of orders that used the code, the nightly count repair recounts it from the orders and puts it right.

event_sessions.purpose: One row per sitting of an event that runs more than once.

columns.seating_zone_id: Set when the session only uses part of the venue
columns.position: Display order; the application renumbers from 0 on every save

notes: A single-sitting event has no row here. Nothing is sold per session yet.

examples.intro: A session is one sitting of an event that runs more than once, such as each performance of a weekend show. A single-sitting event has no rows here, and nothing is sold per session yet: tickets are for the event as a whole.

groups.name: Which session
groups.text: A session belongs to one event, and its name is unique inside that event. `position` sets the order the sessions are listed in.

event_id.means: The [[events]] row this is a sitting of. Deleting the event deletes its sessions with it.

name.means: What the sitting is called. Two sessions of the same event can't share a name.

position.means: Where the session comes in its event's list. Lower numbers come first, starting at `0`. The application renumbers an event's sessions from 0 on every save, in one statement.

created_at.means: When the session was first saved.

groups.name: When and where it runs
groups.text: Each session has its own start and end, written in UTC (`+00`) like every timestamp here. The database checks that a session ends after it starts.

ends_at.means: When it ends. Always after `starts_at`, or the row is refused.

seating_zone_id.means: The [[seating_zones]] row for the part of the venue this sitting uses, set when it only uses part of it. NULL means the whole venue, or that the zone it named has since been deleted.
examples: only the Balcony at Harbour Hall

records.name: The first sitting
records.text: Uses the whole of Harbour Hall, so `seating_zone_id` is empty. First in the list, so `position` is `0`.

records.name: Later the same day
records.text: The same event and the same day, with its own times.

records.name: Part of the venue only
records.text: Uses only the Balcony, so it points at that zone. It was added two days after the other two.

scenarios.title: The Balcony zone is deleted
scenarios.text: Harbour Hall removes its Balcony zone. The Sunday morning session stays, with `seating_zone_id` cleared.

scenarios.title: A session is moved up the list
scenarios.text: Sunday morning is moved to the top and the list is saved. The application renumbers every session of the event from 0, so Sunday morning becomes `0`, Saturday morning `1` and Saturday afternoon `2`.

scenarios.title: Someone tries to delete the event
scenarios.text: Deleting an event deletes its sessions with it. Family Puppet Weekend has orders, though, and an event with orders can't be deleted, so its three sessions stay.

events.purpose: One row per event on sale.

columns.created_by: The organizer who first saved it. NULL once their account is deleted
columns.slug: Used in the public URL, unique inside the organization
columns.status: `sold_out` is set by the checkout job, not by hand
columns.timezone: IANA name. All the timestamps are absolute; this is how they are shown
columns.cancelled_at: Set together with `status = 'cancelled'`; refunds are queued from here

notes: An event can't be deleted while an organization still exists for it, and the organization can't be deleted while it has events.
Cancelling is not deleting: the row stays so tickets, payments and refunds still make sense.

examples.intro: An event is one thing an organization sells tickets for, such as a concert or a show. `status` is the one column that decides whether the public can see it and whether tickets can be bought.

groups.name: Which event
groups.text: Two ids for the same row: one for the database, one for everyone else.

id.means: The internal number. Ticket types, sessions, orders and tickets all join on it. It is never sent to a client.

public_id.means: The event's id outside the server, wherever a client names it. Random, so nobody can guess another event's id or count how many there are from a URL.

groups.name: Whose it is, and where
groups.text: An event always belongs to one organization. It may or may not have a venue.

organization_id.means: The organization selling the event. An organization can't be deleted while it has events.

venue_id.means: The [[venues]] row for where it is held. NULL for an online-only event. A venue can't be deleted while an event, even a cancelled one, still points at it.

created_by.means: The organizer who first saved the event, as a [[users]] row. NULL once that person's account is deleted; the event itself stays.

groups.name: What the public reads
groups.text: `title` and `summary` are the words; `slug` is the readable part of the web address.

slug.means: A *slug* is a short, readable name used in a web address, like `winter-jazz-night`. Up to 80 characters. It is unique inside the organization, not across the platform, so two organizations can each have a `winter-jazz-night`.

summary.means: A short description, when one was written. It can be empty.
examples: An evening of big-band jazz in the main hall.

groups.name: Where it is in its life
groups.text: An event moves `draft` → `on_sale` → `sold_out` → `completed`, and can be `cancelled` from any step. The two timestamps say when it was published and when it was cancelled.

status.means: Where the event is now. It decides whether the public can see the event and whether tickets can be bought.

examples.draft: Still being set up; not on sale.
examples.on_sale: On sale: tickets can be bought.
examples.sold_out: Every ticket type is full. Set by the checkout job when the last type fills, never by hand, and put back to `on_sale` when a refund frees stock.
examples.cancelled: Called off. Possible from any step. The row stays, so its tickets, payments and refunds still make sense.

published_at.means: When the event was published, if it has been. A ticket type with no `sales_start_at` is on sale from this moment.

cancelled_at.means: When the event was cancelled. Set together with `status = 'cancelled'`, and refunds are queued from there. Empty for an event that isn't cancelled.

groups.name: When it happens
text: Every timestamp is an absolute moment, written here in UTC (the `+00` at the end). `timezone` only decides how they are shown: Winter Jazz Night is stored as starting at 19:00 UTC and shown as 20:00 in Amsterdam.
The database checks the order: `ends_at` must be after `starts_at`, and the doors may not open after the start.

timezone.means: How this event's times are shown, as a name from the *IANA time zone database*: the list every operating system uses, written `Region/City`, which also knows when summer time starts and ends. Every event has one, online events too.

examples.Europe/Amsterdam: UTC+1 in winter, UTC+2 in summer
examples.Europe/Lisbon: UTC+0 in winter, UTC+1 in summer

doors_open_at.means: When the doors open. NULL means they open at `starts_at`. Never later than `starts_at`.

ends_at.means: When it ends. Always after `starts_at`, or the row is refused.

created_at.means: When the event was first saved.

updated_at.means: The last change to the row. The application sets it, not a database trigger.

records.name: On sale at a venue
records.text: A one-night concert at Harbour Hall. Its ticket types are rows in [[ticket_types]], and the [[orders]] for it use the same event id.

values.title: Winter Jazz Night
values.summary: An evening of big-band jazz in the main hall.

records.name: An online draft
records.text: Online only, so `venue_id` is empty, but it still has a `timezone`: every event needs one to show its times. Not published yet, and nobody has written a summary.

records.name: Sold out, running three times
records.text: A weekend show with three sittings, which are rows in [[event_sessions]]; nothing is sold per session, only per event. The checkout job set `sold_out` when its last ticket type filled. `doors_open_at` is empty, so the doors open at the start.

values.title: Family Puppet Weekend
values.summary: Three short puppet shows for children and their families.

records.name: Cancelled
records.text: Called off before the night. `cancelled_at` is set and the row stays. Lisbon is on UTC in winter, so the stored times read the same as the local ones. The organizer who created it has since deleted their account, so `created_by` is empty.

values.title: Lakeside Acoustic Night
values.summary: Three acoustic sets on the terrace.

scenarios.title: An event sells out, then a ticket comes back
text: Family Puppet Weekend sells its last ticket. The checkout job sets `sold_out`, because the last of its ticket types has filled.
Later a buyer is refunded, which frees stock, and the event goes back to `on_sale`.

scenarios.title: An event is cancelled
text: Lakeside Acoustic Night is called off. `status` becomes `cancelled` and `cancelled_at` is set with it.
Refunds are queued from there: the cancellation job writes the [[refunds]] rows, with the reason `event_cancelled`. The event row stays.

scenarios.title: Someone tries to delete an event
text: Deleting an event takes its sessions, ticket types, discount codes, attendees, check-ins and waitlist with it.
It is refused while the event has orders. Winter Jazz Night has them, so it stays. A draft nobody has bought from, like Songwriting Q&A, can be deleted.

notifications.purpose: One row per message the platform sent to one person.

columns.event_id: What the message was about. Cleared if the event is deleted, which keeps the send record
columns.status: `skipped` means the person had turned this message off
columns.error: Provider message for a `failed` send, kept for support

examples.intro: A notification is one message to one person: an email, a text or a push message. The row records what was sent, how, and whether it went out.

groups.name: Who it was for
groups.text: Always one person with an account: `user_id` can't be empty.

organization_id.means: The organization the message was sent for. If the organization row is deleted, its notifications go with it.

user_id.means: The person, a row in [[users]]. Their `locale` there decides which language messages are sent in. If their account row is deleted, their notifications go with it.

template_key.means: Which message it was: the name of its template in `app/mailers/`.

event_id.means: The event the message was about, when it was about one. If the event is deleted this is cleared, and the record of the send stays.
examples: the event Priya bought tickets for
the event has since been deleted

scenarios.title: The event is deleted later
scenarios.text: An event the person was messaged about is deleted. The message stays here: only the link is cleared, and the row still says who was sent what, how and when.

examples.sms: A text message to a phone.
examples.push: A push message to a phone or browser signed in through [[user_devices]].

groups.name: What happened to it
groups.text: A new row starts as `queued`, the column's default. The send worker's queue is exactly the `queued` rows.

examples.skipped: Not sent: the person had turned this message off.

sent_at.means: When the message went out. Empty while it is `queued`, and for a `skipped` message, which never went out.

error.means: The provider's message for a `failed` send, kept for support. The *provider* is the outside service that delivers the email, text or push for the platform.

scenarios.title: A send fails
scenarios.text: The mail provider rejects the address. The row stays, with the provider's own words in `error` for support to read.

id.means: The internal number, for joins only. It is never sent to a client.

created_at.means: When the message was queued: the row exists before anything is sent.

records.name: A sent confirmation
records.text: Priya's order confirmation for order 88120, sent by email a few seconds after it was queued.

records.name: Still in the queue
records.text: The waitlist release job has just offered Lena a ticket and queued this push message. The send worker hasn't picked it up yet.

records.name: Skipped
records.text: This person had turned this message off, so the text never went out and `sent_at` is empty.

scenarios.title: A waitlist place opens up
text: The waitlist release job runs every five minutes. It offers freed stock to the oldest `waiting` entry in [[waitlist_entries]], Lena's, and queues a notification: a new row here, `queued`.
The send worker picks it up and sends it.

scenarios.title: A person deletes their account
text: Priya deletes her account. It is hidden at once, and the nightly purge removes the [[users]] row once it has been deleted for more than 30 days.
Her notifications go with that row. `user_id` is a cascading link, unlike `event_id`, which is only cleared.

order_lines.purpose: One row per ticket type in an order, with how many were bought.

columns.line_no: Numbered from 1 inside the order, and never reused
columns.unit_price_cents: The price at the moment of checkout, not today's price
columns.line_total_cents: `unit_price_cents × quantity`, stored so historic orders never move

notes: Editing a paid order is not allowed. A mistake is refunded and bought again.

examples.intro: An order line is one ticket type in an order: how many were bought, and at what price. An order for two kinds of ticket has two lines.

groups.name: Which line
groups.text: A line has no id of its own. Its key is the pair `(order_id, line_no)`: a *composite key*, two columns that only name one row together. [[attendees]] points at a line with both.

order_id.means: The order the line belongs to, from [[orders]]. Deleting the order deletes its lines too.

line_no.means: The line's number inside its order, counting from 1. A number is never reused inside the same order.

groups.name: What was bought
groups.text: One line per ticket type. Each ticket on it becomes its own row in [[attendees]], so a line for 2 makes two tickets.

ticket_type_id.means: The ticket type bought, from [[ticket_types]]. A ticket type that any line points at can't be deleted: the database refuses.

quantity.means: How many tickets of that type. Always at least 1; the database checks it.

groups.name: The money
text: Whole cents, in the order's `currency`: the line has no currency of its own.

The database checks the sum: `line_total_cents` must equal `unit_price_cents × quantity`, or the row is refused. An order's lines added up give its `subtotal_cents`. The table shows Priya's order 88120, which has two lines.

unit_price_cents.means: The price of one ticket at the moment of checkout, not today's price. If the organizer changes the price later, this keeps the old one.

line_total_cents.means: `unit_price_cents × quantity`, stored so a past order's total never moves.

scenarios.title: The price changes after checkout
scenarios.text: The organizer raises General admission at event 3051 from 25.00 to 30.00. Amira's line was priced at checkout, so it keeps the old price, and her order's totals don't move.

records.name: Two tickets of one type
records.text: Amira's order 90412: two General admission tickets at 25.00, on one line. They become two rows in [[attendees]].

records.name: The first of two lines
records.text: Priya's order 88120 mixes two ticket types, so it has two lines. This one is two reserved seats. The order was later partly refunded, but a paid order is never edited, so the line still shows what was bought.

records.name: The second line
records.text: The same order's standing tickets, with `line_no` 2. 7000 + 5000 is the order's `subtotal_cents` of 12000.

records.name: A free ticket
records.text: A `comp` ticket costs nothing, so its price and total are 0. It still needs a line, because every ticket in [[attendees]] hangs off one.

scenarios.title: A paid order has a mistake in it
text: A buyer pays for three tickets but meant to buy two.
Editing a paid order is not allowed, so the line stays as it is. The mistake is refunded, as a row in [[refunds]], and bought again.

scenarios.title: Someone tries to delete a ticket type that has sold
scenarios.text: The organizer tries to delete General admission at event 3051. Amira's line points at it, so the database refuses the delete.

scenarios.title: An order is deleted
scenarios.text: Deleting an order takes its lines with it, and their attendees and check-ins. The delete is refused while a payment or a refund points at the order.

orders.purpose: One row per basket, which becomes a purchase once it is paid.

columns.user_id: NULL for guest checkout, which is most orders
columns.discount_code_id: Cleared if the code is deleted; `discount_cents` keeps the money that was taken off
columns.buyer_email: Where the tickets were sent. The only way to find a guest order
columns.status: `cart` rows are not purchases and are excluded from every report
columns.subtotal_cents: Sum of the order lines, before discount and fee
columns.fee_cents: The platform's cut, taken from `organizations.fee_bps` at checkout
columns.total_cents: What the buyer was charged. The database checks it against the other three
columns.placed_at: Set when the basket is submitted; NULL while `status = 'cart'`
columns.expires_at: When an unpaid basket releases its held tickets

notes: A basket is a row here from the first ticket added, so held stock is visible to everyone.
Abandoned baskets are swept hourly: `status` becomes `expired` and the held quantities go back.

examples.intro: An order is a basket from the moment the first ticket goes in, and a purchase once it is paid. Most of its columns are about money, and every amount is in whole cents.

groups.name: Which order
groups.text: Two ids for the same row: one for the database, one for everyone else.

id.means: The internal number. Other tables join on it; it is never sent to a browser or the app.

public_id.means: The order's id outside the server: in receipt links, emails and the API. Random, so nobody can guess another order's id or count how many there are.

groups.name: Who is buying, and what for
groups.text: An order is always for one event. The buyer may or may not have an account.

event_id.means: The event the tickets are for. One order never mixes events.

user_id.means: The signed-in buyer, when there is one. NULL for guest checkout, which is most orders.

buyer_email.means: Where the tickets were sent. For a guest order it is the only way to find the order again, so it is required even when `user_id` is set.

buyer_name.means: The buyer's name, when one was given. It can be empty.

groups.name: Where it is in its life
groups.text: `status` says what the order is right now; the two timestamps say when it was submitted and when an unpaid basket gives up.

status.means: What the order is right now. Only `cart` rows are not purchases, and every report leaves them out.

examples.cart: A basket still being filled. Its tickets are held, but nothing is bought yet.
examples.pending: Submitted; waiting for the payment to go through.
examples.partially_refunded: Some of the money has gone back to the buyer.
examples.refunded: All of the money has gone back.
examples.expired: An unpaid basket the hourly sweeper closed; its held tickets went back on sale.

placed_at.means: When the basket was submitted. NULL while the order is still a `cart`, and for a basket that expired without being submitted.

expires_at.means: When an unpaid basket gives back the tickets it is holding.

groups.name: The money
text: Every amount is whole cents in the order's `currency`, so 47.25 euros is stored as `4725`. Whole numbers never pick up rounding errors the way decimals can.
The database itself checks the sum: `total_cents` must equal `subtotal_cents − discount_cents + fee_cents`, or the row is refused.

currency.means: The three-letter currency code (ISO 4217) every amount on this row is in.

subtotal_cents.means: The order lines added up, before any discount or fee.

discount_code_id.means: The discount code the buyer entered, if any. If the code is deleted later this is cleared, but `discount_cents` keeps the amount that was taken off.

discount_cents.means: How much the discount took off. `0` when no code was used.

fee_cents.means: The platform's cut, worked out from the organization's `fee_bps` (basis points: 100 = 1%) at checkout.

head: Column
Value
Why
rows: The platform's cut, from the organization's `fee_bps`

scenarios.title: The discount code is deleted later
scenarios.text: The organizer deletes SPRING10 after the sale ends. The order keeps the money that was taken off; only the link to the code goes.

created_at.means: When the row was made: the moment the first ticket went into the basket, not when it was paid.

updated_at.means: The last change to the row. The application sets it, not a database trigger.

records.name: A paid guest order
records.text: Amira buys two tickets without an account, using the code SPRING10.

records.name: A basket in progress
records.text: Jonas, who has an account, has one ticket in his basket and hasn't checked out yet. The fee is only worked out at checkout.

records.name: An expired basket
records.text: Someone filled a basket and left. The sweeper closed it after `expires_at`; the row stays, but it was never a purchase.

records.name: A partly refunded order
records.text: A paid order for four tickets, where one ticket's money has gone back. The refund itself is a row in [[refunds]].

scenarios.title: A buyer abandons a basket
text: Sam adds three tickets and closes the tab. The row has existed since the first ticket went in, so those tickets are held from everyone else.
Once `expires_at` has passed, the hourly basket sweeper closes the basket and gives the held tickets back.

scenarios.title: A guest checks out
scenarios.text: Amira submits her basket without signing in, and her payment goes through.

scenarios.title: Some of the money goes back
scenarios.text: Priya returns one of her four tickets. A [[refunds]] row records the money, and the order moves on from `paid`.

org_members.purpose: One row per person who may act for an organization.

columns.role: What this person may do in the organizer dashboard
columns.invited_by: Who sent the invitation. NULL once that account is deleted
columns.accepted_at: NULL while the invitation is still outstanding

notes: No surrogate key: the pair of ids is the primary key, so one person can hold one role per organization.

examples.intro: One row says that one person may act for one organization, and in which role. The row is there from the moment the invitation is sent; `accepted_at` says whether it has been taken up.

groups.name: Who, and for which organization
text: There is no `id` column. The pair of ids *is* the key, so one person holds one role per organization.
The same person can still belong to several organizations, with a different role in each.

organization_id.means: The organization the person may act for. If the organization is deleted for real, its memberships go with it.

user_id.means: The person, in [[users]]. It can't be empty, so even an invitation nobody has accepted yet names an existing account. If that account is deleted for real, the membership goes with it.

head: organization_id
user_id
role
What it shows
rows: Ana again, at a venue group's sub-account, with another role

role.means: What this person may do in the organizer dashboard. The database only checks that it is one of these five names; what each one allows is decided by the application.

examples.organizer: Someone who works on the organization's events.
examples.finance: Someone who looks after the organization's money.
examples.viewer: Someone who may look at the dashboard.

scenarios.title: A member's role is changed
scenarios.text: Leo moves from `viewer` to `organizer`. His row is changed in place: there can't be a second row for the same person and organization. [[audit_log]] gets an entry with the action `role_changed`.

groups.name: The invitation
groups.text: Each row records an invitation: who sent it, when, and when it was accepted. While `accepted_at` is empty the invitation is outstanding, and it appears in the organization's list of outstanding invitations.

invited_by.means: Who sent the invitation, in [[users]]. NULL once that account is deleted; the membership itself stays.
examples: the inviter's account has since been deleted

invited_at.means: When the invitation was sent. If nothing else is given, the database fills in the moment the row is made.

accepted_at.means: When the person accepted. NULL while the invitation is still outstanding.

scenarios.title: An invitation is accepted
scenarios.text: Mei invites Leo as a `viewer`. His row is there at once, with `accepted_at` empty. When he accepts, `accepted_at` gets the time.

records.name: A member who accepted
records.text: Mei invited Ana to Lakeside Jazz Club as an `organizer`, and Ana accepted the same afternoon.

records.name: An invitation still outstanding
records.text: Mei invited Leo on 25 November. Until he accepts, `accepted_at` stays empty and the invitation is listed among the organization's outstanding ones.

records.name: The inviter's account is gone
records.text: Tom was invited by someone whose account has since been deleted. `invited_by` was cleared; Tom's membership and role are untouched.

scenarios.title: A member's account is deleted
text: Mei's [[users]] row is removed for real. Her own membership, as owner of Lakeside Jazz Club, goes with it.
The memberships she sent invitations for stay. Ana's and Leo's rows keep their roles, with `invited_by` cleared.

organizations.purpose: One row per organizer account that sells tickets.

columns.parent_org_id: Set for a venue group's sub-accounts, which share billing. NULL for a standalone organizer
columns.slug: Used in the public URL and unique across the whole platform
columns.plan: Decides the feature flags, not the fee
columns.payout_currency: Payouts are made in this currency; events may still sell in another
columns.fee_bps: Platform fee in basis points, copied onto each order at checkout
columns.deleted_at: Hides the organization. Events, orders and payments are kept

notes: The tenant root: almost everything else is reachable from a row here.

examples.intro: One row is one organizer account that sells tickets. It is the tenant root: almost every other row in the database can be traced back to an organization.

groups.name: Which organization
groups.text: Three ways to name the same row: an internal number for joins, a random id for everyone outside the server, and a readable `slug` for the web address.

id.means: The internal number. Other tables join on it; it is never sent to a browser or the app.

public_id.means: The organization's id outside the server. Random, so nobody can guess another organization's id or count how many there are.

slug.means: The short name in the organization's public web address (URL), at most 63 characters. It is unique across the whole platform, not just inside one account. The rule counts hidden (soft-deleted) organizations too, so a slug stays taken for as long as its row exists.

scenarios.title: A second organization asks for a slug that is taken
scenarios.text: A new organizer tries to use `lakeside-jazz-club`. The database refuses the row, because that slug already belongs to organization 12.

groups.name: Part of a venue group
groups.text: A venue group runs several sub-accounts under one parent organization, and they share billing. The parent is just another row in this same table.

parent_org_id.means: The parent organization, for a venue group's sub-account. NULL for a standalone organizer.
examples: a sub-account of Example Venue Group

scenarios.title: The parent organization is deleted
scenarios.text: When the parent row is deleted for real, its sub-accounts stay, with `parent_org_id` cleared. Nothing cascades.

groups.name: Plan, currency and fee
text: `plan` switches features on and off. It does not set the fee: that is `fee_bps`, on the same row.
`fee_bps` is in *basis points*, hundredths of a percent: `100` is 1%, and the default `250` is 2.5%. The database refuses anything outside 0 to 2000, which is 0% to 20%.

plan.means: Which plan the organization is on. It decides the feature flags (the switches in the application that turn features on or off), not the fee.

examples.free: Where every new organization starts: it is the column's default.
examples.pro: Switches on the features the application ties to `pro`.
examples.enterprise: Switches on the features the application ties to `enterprise`.

payout_currency.means: The three-letter currency code (ISO 4217, the international list of currency codes) the organization's payouts are made in. Its events may still sell tickets in another currency.

fee_bps.means: The platform's fee, in basis points (100 = 1%). It is copied onto each order at checkout, so changing it later never changes an order already placed.

scenarios.title: The fee is changed
scenarios.text: Lakeside Jazz Club's fee is lowered from `500` to `400`. Orders it has already sold keep the 5% fee they were charged; only checkouts from now on use 4%.

groups.name: Timestamps and deletion
groups.text: Organizations are soft-deleted: deleting one sets `deleted_at` and hides it, while its events, orders and payments are kept.

created_at.means: When the organization's row was made.

updated_at.means: The last change to the row. The application sets it, not a database trigger.

deleted_at.means: When the organization was deleted. Setting it hides the organization at once (a *soft delete*); its events, orders and payments are kept. The nightly purge job removes rows soft-deleted more than 30 days ago.

records.name: A standalone organizer
records.text: Lakeside Jazz Club sells its own events, with no parent. It is the organizer behind the sample rows in [[orders]]: paid out in euros, with a 5% fee.

records.name: A venue group's sub-account
records.text: Riverside Hall is one of the sub-accounts under Example Venue Group (organization 40). They share billing through the parent.

records.name: A new organization on the defaults
records.text: Every column left out when the row was made took its default: plan `free`, payouts in US dollars, and a 2.5% fee.

records.name: A deleted organization
records.text: Hidden since 2 November, but the row is still here, so its slug is still taken. The nightly purge job removes rows soft-deleted more than 30 days ago.

scenarios.title: An organization is deleted
text: Deleting an organization sets `deleted_at`. It is hidden at once, and its events, orders and payments are all kept.

The nightly purge job removes rows soft-deleted more than 30 days ago. Removing the row for real is refused while the organization still has events, orders, payments or payout batches. Its members, venues, discount codes and [[audit_log]] entries don't stop it: they go with the row.

payments.purpose: One row per attempt to charge a buyer.

columns.payout_batch_id: Set when the payment is swept into a payout. NULL until then
columns.provider_charge_id: The processor's own id, unique per provider. NULL for an attempt that never reached them
columns.status: `disputed` is set from a provider webhook and never by the application
columns.failure_code: The provider's code for a `failed` attempt

notes: A failed attempt stays. An order can have several rows here and at most one that succeeded.
Nothing here is ever deleted: both the order and the organization refuse to go while payments exist.

examples.intro: A payment is one attempt to charge a buyer for an order. A declined card is a row too, so an order can have several attempts here, and at most one of them succeeded.

groups.name: Which payment
groups.text: Two ids for the same row, as on [[orders]]: one for the database, one for everyone else.

id.means: The internal number. Other tables join on it; it is never sent to a client.

public_id.means: The payment's id outside the server. Random, so nobody can guess another payment's id or count how many there are.

groups.name: What it pays for
groups.text: Every attempt is against one order. Neither the order nor the organization can be deleted while a payment points at it, so rows here are never deleted.

organization_id.means: The organization selling the tickets. It can't be deleted while it has payments.

order_id.means: The order this attempt tries to pay for. Failed attempts stay, so one order can have several rows here, and at most one that succeeded.

groups.name: Who took the money
groups.text: A *payment processor* is the outside company that actually charges the buyer's card or account and moves the money, such as Stripe or PayPal.

provider_charge_id.means: The processor's own id for this charge (its *charge id*). The pair `provider` + `provider_charge_id` is unique, so the same charge is never recorded twice. NULL for an attempt that never reached the processor.
examples: the attempt never reached the processor

groups.name: How much
groups.text: Whole cents in the payment's own `currency`, like every amount in this database: 47.25 euros is stored as `4725`.

amount_cents.means: What this attempt tried to charge. The database refuses `0` or less.

currency.means: The three-letter currency code (ISO 4217) that `amount_cents` is in.

groups.name: How it went
groups.text: A new attempt starts as `pending`, the column's default. `failure_code` and `paid_at` say how it ended.

examples.pending: Started; the outcome isn't known yet.
examples.succeeded: The money was taken. Succeeded payments are the ones the weekly payout sweep picks up.
examples.failed: The charge didn't go through. The row stays, with the processor's reason in `failure_code`.
examples.disputed: The buyer has challenged the charge with their bank or the processor (a *chargeback*). Set from a *webhook*, a message the processor sends to the platform, and never by the application.

failure_code.means: The processor's short code for why a `failed` attempt failed. Only a failed attempt has one.

examples.insufficient_funds: not enough money on the card
examples.expired_card: the card is past its expiry date

created_at.means: When the attempt was started and the row was made.

groups.name: Passing the money on
text: Takings reach the organizer in batches. The weekly payout sweep opens a [[payout_batches]] row per organization and sets `payout_batch_id` on the succeeded payments inside the period.
Until then a succeeded payment has no batch. An index lists exactly those rows, by organization and `paid_at`, so the next sweep can find them.

payout_batch_id.means: The payout this payment's money went out in. NULL until the sweep picks it up. A payment is in at most one batch; if that batch row were deleted, this would be cleared and the payment kept.

scenarios.title: The weekly sweep picks a payment up
scenarios.text: Order 88120's payment succeeded on 20 November. The sweep opens batch 418 for organization 12, for 16–22 November, and sets `payout_batch_id` on this payment along with the week's other succeeded ones.

records.name: Paid, not paid out yet
records.text: Amira's order 90412, charged through Stripe on 27 November. The weekly sweep hasn't picked it up yet, so `payout_batch_id` is empty.

records.name: Paid, and paid out
records.text: Priya's order 88120, paid through PayPal and swept into organization 12's payout for 16–22 November. The ticket refunded later is a row in [[refunds]] pointing at this payment; there is no refunded status here.

records.name: A declined card
records.text: Tomás's first card for order 90431 was declined. The attempt reached Stripe, so it has a charge id, and it stays as a `failed` row next to the attempt that worked.

scenarios.title: A card is declined, then another one works
text: Tomás's first card is declined. That attempt stays, as `failed` with the processor's code.
He tries a second card and it goes through. That is a second row for the same order, with its own charge id, and the only one of the two that `succeeded`.

scenarios.title: A buyer disputes a charge
scenarios.text: Some time later, a buyer challenges a charge with their bank. The processor tells the platform through a webhook, and that webhook is what sets `disputed`: the application never does.

payout_batches.purpose: One row per transfer of takings to an organizer.

columns.period_start: First day of takings in this batch, inclusive
columns.period_end: Last day of takings in this batch, inclusive
columns.gross_cents: Sum of the successful payments swept into the batch
columns.fee_cents: Sum of the platform fees on those payments
columns.net_cents: What was actually sent. The database checks it against the other two
columns.status: `sent` means handed to the bank; `paid` means the bank confirmed it

examples.intro: A payout batch is one transfer of takings to an organizer: the succeeded payments of one period added up, minus the platform's fees on them.

id.means: The internal number. Each [[payments]] row swept into this batch points at it through `payout_batch_id`.

organization_id.means: The organization being paid. It can't be deleted while it has payout batches.

groups.name: Which takings it covers
text: Both dates are included: a batch for 16–22 November covers every day from the 16th to the 22nd. They are plain dates, with no time of day.
The database refuses a period that ends before it starts, and a second batch for the same organization with the same two dates.

period_start.means: The first day of takings in this batch, included.

period_end.means: The last day of takings in this batch, included. It may be the same day as `period_start`, never earlier.

scenarios.title: The same period twice
scenarios.text: Organization 12 already has batch 418 for 16–22 November. Another row for organization 12 with those same two dates would be refused by the database.

groups.name: The money
text: *Gross* is the money before the platform's fees come off; *net* is what the organizer actually receives. All three amounts are whole cents in the batch's `currency`, so 12,500.00 euros is `1250000`.
The database checks the sum: `net_cents` must equal `gross_cents − fee_cents`, or the row is refused.

gross_cents.means: The succeeded payments swept into the batch, added up.

fee_cents.means: The platform's fees on those same payments, added up.

net_cents.means: What was actually sent to the organizer.

currency.means: The three-letter currency code (ISO 4217) the amounts are in. An organization's payouts are made in its `payout_currency` on [[organizations]], even when its events sell in another.

Value
Why
rows: Organization 12's succeeded payments for 16–22 November, order 88120's 12600 among them
The platform's fees on those payments, order 88120's 600 among them

groups.name: Where the transfer is
groups.text: `status` follows the transfer from the batch being opened to the bank confirming it.

status.means: Where the transfer stands. A new batch starts as `open`, the column's default.

examples.open: Opened by the weekly payout sweep; not handed to the bank yet.
examples.failed: The transfer did not go through.

sent_at.means: When the batch was handed to the bank. Empty while it is still `open`.

records.name: Paid out
records.text: Organization 12's takings for 16–22 November, including Priya's order 88120. The bank has confirmed the transfer.

records.name: Sent, not yet confirmed
records.text: An organizer paid out in pounds. The batch is with the bank, which hasn't confirmed it yet.

records.name: Still open
records.text: Opened by the sweep but not handed to the bank yet, so `sent_at` is empty.

scenarios.title: A week's takings are paid out
text: The weekly payout sweep opens batch 418 for organization 12, for 16–22 November, and sets `payout_batch_id` on that period's succeeded [[payments]], order 88120's among them.
The batch is handed to the bank and becomes `sent`. Once the bank confirms the transfer, it is `paid`.

refunds.purpose: One row per amount sent back to a buyer.

columns.order_id: Carried so refunds can be totalled per order without joining `payments`
columns.requested_by: The staff member who asked for it. NULL for an automatic refund after a cancellation
columns.amount_cents: May be less than the payment: partial refunds are normal

notes: Several partial refunds against one payment are allowed. The application keeps their sum within the payment.

examples.intro: A refund is money sent back to a buyer, against one payment. Refunds can be partial, and one payment can have several of them.

groups.name: What the money goes back against
groups.text: Each refund points at the [[payments]] row whose money it returns, and at that payment's order as well.

id.means: The internal number, for joins only. It is never sent to a client.

payment_id.means: The payment whose money goes back. If that payment row were deleted its refunds would go with it, but payments are never deleted.

order_id.means: The order the payment was for. It repeats what `payment_id` already leads to, so refunds can be totalled per order without joining [[payments]]. An order can't be deleted while a refund points at it.

groups.name: Who asked, and why
groups.text: `requested_by` says which staff member asked for the refund; `reason` says why the money went back.

requested_by.means: The staff member who asked for the refund, a row in [[users]]. NULL for an automatic refund after a cancellation. If that person's account row is deleted, this is cleared and the refund stays.

examples.requested_by_buyer: The buyer asked for their money back.
examples.event_cancelled: The event was cancelled. Written by the cancellation job, not by a person, so `requested_by` is NULL.
examples.fraud: A fraud case. Besides sending the money back, this closes the order and voids its tickets in [[attendees]], and a void ticket is refused at the door.

groups.name: How much
groups.text: Whole cents, so 30.00 is stored as `3000`. The row has no `currency` column; the payment it points at has one.

amount_cents.means: How much goes back. It may be less than the payment: partial refunds are normal. The database refuses `0` or less.
examples: one 30.00 ticket out of the 126.00 paid for order 88120

scenarios.title: A second ticket goes back
text: Suppose Priya later returns a second ticket. That is a second refund row against the same payment, with its own amount.
The database only checks that each amount is above zero. Keeping the refunds' sum within the payment is the application's job: here 3000 + 3000, well inside 12600.

groups.name: Where it stands
groups.text: A new refund starts as `pending`, the column's default.

status.means: Whether the money has gone back yet.

examples.failed: The refund did not go through.

settled_at.means: When the refund was settled. Empty while it is still `pending`.

records.name: A partial refund a buyer asked for
records.text: Priya returns one of her four 30.00 tickets on order 88120. Staff member 1043 asked for the refund, and the money has gone back.

records.name: After a cancellation
records.text: Event 3112 has just been cancelled. The cancellation job wrote this refund, so nobody is named in `requested_by`, and it hasn't settled yet.

records.name: A fraud case
records.text: Order 90290 turned out to be fraudulent. The refund sends the money back, and because the reason is `fraud`, the order is closed and its tickets are voided too.

scenarios.title: Some of the money goes back
scenarios.text: Priya returns one of her four tickets. A staff member asks for a refund of that ticket's 30.00 against her payment, and the order moves from `paid` to `partially_refunded`.

scenarios.title: An event is cancelled
text: The organizer cancels event 3112. Refunds are queued from the event's cancellation, and the cancellation job writes them.
No staff member asked, so `requested_by` is NULL and `reason` is `event_cancelled`.

seating_zones.purpose: One row per named part of a venue, such as a stand or a tier.

columns.capacity: Seats in this zone. The sum across zones may be below the venue's own `capacity`
columns.position: Display order; the application renumbers from 0 on every save

notes: Deleting a zone leaves its ticket types and sessions in place with an empty zone.

examples.intro: A seating zone is a named part of one venue, such as a stand, a tier or a balcony. Reserved ticket types point at a zone, and so does a session that only uses part of the room.

groups.name: Which zone, in which venue
groups.text: A zone belongs to one venue, and its name is unique inside that venue.

id.means: The internal number. [[ticket_types]] and [[event_sessions]] point at it.

venue_id.means: The venue this zone is part of. Deleting the venue deletes its zones with it.

name.means: What the zone is called. Harbour Hall can have only one zone called Balcony; another venue can have a Balcony of its own.

created_at.means: When the zone was first saved.

groups.name: Size and order
text: `capacity` is how many people the zone holds. A venue's zones don't have to add up to the venue's own `capacity` on [[venues]]: the sum may be below it.
At Harbour Hall the two zones hold 1100 together, while the venue as a whole holds 1200.

capacity.means: How many people this zone holds. Always at least 1: the database refuses `0` or less.

position.means: Where the zone comes in its venue's list of zones. Lower numbers come first, starting at `0`. The application renumbers a venue's zones from 0 on every save, in one statement, so after a save they always run 0, 1, 2…
