scenarios.text: Deleting Harbour Hall would delete both of its zones with it. While any event still points at the venue, though, the venue can't be deleted, so its zones stay too.

ticket_types.purpose: One row per thing a buyer can put in a basket.

columns.seating_zone_id: Set for `reserved` types. Cleared if the zone is deleted
columns.kind: Decides whether a seat label is assigned and whether money is taken
columns.price_cents: `0` for `comp` tickets, which still create attendees
columns.quantity_total: How many may ever be sold, including the ones already sold
columns.quantity_sold: Raised inside the checkout transaction; the database refuses to let it pass `quantity_total`
columns.max_per_order: Per-basket cap shown on the ticket page
columns.sales_start_at: NULL means on sale as soon as the event is published
columns.sales_end_at: NULL means on sale until the event starts
columns.position: Display order on the ticket page; renumbered from 0 on every save

notes: Price and name can change. Sold orders keep their own copy, so changing them never moves a past total.

examples.intro: A ticket type is one thing a buyer can put in a basket: a name, a price and how many there are, such as *General admission* or *Balcony seat*. An event can have several, listed on its ticket page in `position` order.

groups.name: Which ticket type
groups.text: A ticket type belongs to one event, and its name is unique inside that event.

id.means: The internal number. [[order_lines]], [[attendees]] and [[waitlist_entries]] point at it. It is never sent to a client.

public_id.means: The type's id outside the server, wherever a client names it. Random, so nobody can guess or count ids from a URL.

event_id.means: The event it sells tickets for. Deleting the event deletes its ticket types, but an event with orders can't be deleted.

created_at.means: When the type was first saved.

groups.name: What the buyer picks
groups.text: `kind` decides whether each ticket gets a seat label and whether money is taken. `position` sets the order on the ticket page.

name.means: What the buyer sees in the list. It can be changed later.

kind.means: What sort of ticket it is. It decides whether a seat label is assigned and whether money is taken.

examples.general: General admission: no seat is assigned, so the tickets have no seat label.
examples.reserved: A seat in a particular zone: `seating_zone_id` points at the zone, and each ticket in [[attendees]] gets a seat label.
examples.vip: A VIP ticket. Like `general`, it gets no seat label: only `reserved` tickets have one.
examples.comp: Short for *complimentary*: a free ticket. `price_cents` is `0`, but each one still creates an [[attendees]] row, like a paid ticket.

seating_zone_id.means: The [[seating_zones]] row these seats are in. Set for `reserved` types, empty for the others. Cleared if the zone is deleted, so a `reserved` type can end up with no zone.

position.means: Where the type comes on the ticket page. Lower numbers come first, starting at `0`. The application renumbers an event's types from 0 on every save.

groups.name: The price
groups.text: Whole cents in the row's own `currency`, so 25.00 euros is stored as `2500`. Like all money in this database: no floats, and the currency is always on the same row, never assumed.

price_cents.means: The price of one ticket, in cents. Never negative; `0` for `comp` tickets. Orders already sold keep their own copy in [[order_lines]] (`unit_price_cents`), so changing it never moves a past total.

currency.means: The three-letter currency code (ISO 4217) the price is in. It can differ from the organization's `payout_currency`: an event may sell in one currency and be paid out in another.

scenarios.title: The price goes up
scenarios.text: General admission goes from 25.00 to 30.00. Amira's paid order keeps 25.00 on its [[order_lines]] row, so her total doesn't move.

groups.name: How many can be sold
text: `quantity_total` is the whole stock and `quantity_sold` is how much of it is taken. The database refuses a row where `quantity_sold` is below 0 or above `quantity_total`, and the ticket page lists as buyable only the types with some left.

`quantity_sold` is a *stored count*: a running total kept on the row so the ticket page doesn't count orders on every view. The checkout transaction moves it, and a nightly job recounts it from the orders and corrects any drift.

quantity_total.means: How many may ever be sold, including the ones already sold.

quantity_sold.means: How many are taken. Raised inside the checkout transaction. Tickets held in an unpaid basket count too: when the basket sweeper closes an expired basket, it lowers this by what the basket held.

max_per_order.means: The most of this type one basket may hold, shown on the ticket page. At least 1, and `10` unless set otherwise.

scenarios.title: Two buyers want the last VIP ticket
scenarios.text: VIP lounge has 49 of 50 sold, and two buyers check out at the same moment. Each checkout raises `quantity_sold` inside its transaction, but the database won't let it pass `quantity_total`, so whichever comes second is refused.

groups.name: When it is on sale
groups.text: Two optional dates. Left empty, a type is on sale from the moment the event is published until the event starts.

sales_start_at.means: When this type goes on sale. NULL means as soon as the event is published.
examples: a week after the event was published

sales_end_at.means: When this type stops selling. NULL means on sale until the event starts.
examples: an hour before the doors open

records.name: General admission
records.text: Unreserved tickets at 25.00 EUR, the ones in Amira's order in [[orders]]. Both sales dates are empty, so it sells from publishing until the event starts.

records.name: A reserved seat
records.text: Seats in Harbour Hall's Balcony zone, so each ticket gets a seat label. It went on sale a week after the event was published and stops an hour before the doors open.

records.name: A full type
records.text: `quantity_sold` has reached `quantity_total`, so it is no longer listed as buyable. The event stays `on_sale`: it only becomes `sold_out` when its last ticket type fills.

records.name: Free guest tickets
records.text: A `comp` type: the price is `0` and no money is taken, but every ticket still becomes an [[attendees]] row with its own barcode.

scenarios.title: A basket is abandoned
text: Sam puts three General admission tickets in a basket and leaves. The basket is already a real [[orders]] row, and its three tickets count in `quantity_sold`.
Once the basket's `expires_at` has passed, the hourly basket sweeper closes it and lowers `quantity_sold` by three, so those tickets can be bought again.

scenarios.title: Someone tries to delete a type that has sold
text: General admission has been bought, so [[order_lines]] and [[attendees]] rows point at it. Those links refuse the delete, and the row stays.
A type nobody has bought can be deleted. A [[waitlist_entries]] row waiting for it just has its `ticket_type_id` cleared.

scenarios.title: Its zone is deleted
scenarios.text: Harbour Hall removes its Balcony zone. *Balcony seat* stays, still `reserved`, with `seating_zone_id` cleared.

user_devices.purpose: One row per phone or browser signed in for push messages.

columns.platform: Which push service the token belongs to
columns.push_token: The provider's token. Unique across the platform, because the provider reissues it
columns.label: Device name the person can recognise in their settings
columns.last_seen_at: Last time the app opened. Tokens unused for 90 days are deleted

examples.intro: One row is one phone or browser where a person has signed in for push messages: the alerts that pop up on a phone's screen or from a browser. One person can have several.

user_id.means: The person the device belongs to, in [[users]]. If their account is deleted for real, the device goes with it.

label.means: A device name the person can recognise in their settings. It can be empty.

groups.name: Where push messages go
groups.text: Each platform has its own push service. The *push token* is what that service hands out for one device: a message sent to the token reaches that phone or browser.

platform.means: Which push service the token belongs to.

examples.ios: An iPhone or iPad. The token is for Apple's push service.
examples.android: An Android phone or tablet. The token is for Google's push service.
examples.web: A web browser. The token is for that browser's push service.

push_token.means: The provider's token for this device. It is unique across the whole platform, because the provider reissues it: the same token can never sit on two rows.
examples: an Android token, made up and shortened

groups.name: How recently it was used
groups.text: Devices nobody uses are cleaned up: the nightly purge deletes tokens unused for 90 days.

last_seen_at.means: The last time the app opened on this device. When that is more than 90 days ago, the nightly purge deletes the row.

created_at.means: When the device's row was made.

scenarios.title: A phone is put away
scenarios.text: Mei stops using her old Android phone, so its `last_seen_at` stops moving. Once 90 days have passed with no use, the nightly purge deletes the row.

records.name: A phone in daily use
records.text: Jonas's iPhone, last opened on the evening of 27 November.

records.name: A browser with no label
records.text: Mei also gets push messages in a web browser. No device name was given for it, so `label` is empty.

records.name: An old phone about to go
records.text: Not opened since 2 September. If it stays unused, the nightly purge deletes it once 90 days have passed, at the start of December.

scenarios.title: The person's account is deleted
scenarios.text: When Mei's [[users]] row is removed for real, both of her devices go with it: the browser and the old phone.

users.purpose: One row per person with a sign-in, whether buyer or organizer.

columns.email: Unique case-insensitively, through a unique index on `lower(email)`
columns.locale: Which language messages are sent in
columns.password_set_at: NULL for an account that has only ever used a magic link
columns.deleted_at: Hides the account. Orders and tickets stay, with the link cleared

notes: Most buyers never have a row here: guest checkout only stores `orders.buyer_email`.

examples.intro: One row is one person who can sign in, whether they buy tickets or run an organization. Most buyers never get a row here: a guest checkout only keeps the email on the order.

groups.name: Which account
groups.text: Two ids for the same person: one for the database, one for everyone else.

id.means: The internal number. Other tables join on it; it is never sent to a browser or the app.

public_id.means: The account's id outside the server. Random, so nobody can guess another account's id or count the accounts.

groups.name: Who they are
groups.text: The email is the one thing every account must have. The name is optional.

email.means: The address the person signs in with. No two accounts can share one, even with different capitals: a unique index on `lower(email)` compares addresses in lower case. The database's only other check is that there is something before the `@`.

full_name.means: The person's name, when one was given. It can be empty.

locale.means: Which language messages to this person are sent in, as a short language code. English (`en`) is the default.

scenarios.title: The same address with different capitals
scenarios.text: Someone tries to make a second account as `Jonas.Weber@Example.com`. The database refuses it: in lower case, that address already belongs to Jonas.

groups.name: Signing in
groups.text: A person can sign in with a *magic link* (a one-time sign-in link) or with a password. Nothing on this row says what they may do for an organization: that is in [[org_members]].

password_set_at.means: When a password was set on the account. NULL for an account that has only ever used a magic link.

last_seen_at.means: When the person was last active. Support and the activity report use it to list recently active accounts.

groups.name: Created and deleted
groups.text: Accounts are soft-deleted: deleting one sets `deleted_at` and hides it, and the row itself goes later.

deleted_at.means: When the account was deleted. Setting it hides the account at once (a *soft delete*). The nightly purge job removes the row for good once it has been deleted for more than 30 days.

records.name: A buyer who uses magic links
records.text: Jonas buys tickets with his account and has never set a password, so `password_set_at` is empty. The basket in progress on the [[orders]] tab is his.

records.name: An organizer with a password
records.text: Mei runs Lakeside Jazz Club. Her role there is a row in [[org_members]], not a column here: the account itself looks just like a buyer's.

records.name: A deleted account
records.text: Hidden since 10 November, but the row is still here, and everything that points at it still does. The nightly purge removes it once more than 30 days have passed.

scenarios.title: An account is deleted
text: Noor's account is deleted. `deleted_at` is set and the account is hidden straight away; nothing else changes yet.

Once it has been deleted for more than 30 days, the nightly purge removes the row. Her orders stay, with their lines, tickets and payments, and only `user_id` is cleared; the buyer's email stays on each order. Her memberships in [[org_members]], her devices in [[user_devices]] and her [[notifications]] go with the row. Other rows that name her, such as [[audit_log]] entries or door scans in [[check_ins]], stay with the link cleared.

scenarios.title: A magic-link account gets a password
scenarios.text: Jonas has only ever signed in with magic links, so `password_set_at` is empty. Once he sets a password, it holds the moment he did.

venues.purpose: One row per place an organization puts events on.

columns.timezone: IANA name, used to show times for events held here
columns.capacity: Whole-venue limit. NULL when nobody has filled it in
columns.latitude: Set by geocoding the address, not typed in
columns.longitude: Set by geocoding the address, not typed in

notes: A venue can't be deleted while an event still points at it.

examples.intro: A venue is a place where an organization puts on events: a hall, a club, a theatre. It belongs to one organization, and its [[seating_zones]] split the room into named parts.

groups.name: Which venue, and whose
groups.text: A venue belongs to one organization, and its name is unique inside that organization.

id.means: The internal number. [[events]] and [[seating_zones]] point at it. Like every `id` in this database, it is for joins only and never sent to a client.

organization_id.means: The organization that owns the venue. Deleting the organization deletes its venues, and their seating zones, with it.

name.means: What the venue is called. One organization can't have two venues with the same name; two different organizations can.

created_at.means: When the venue was first saved.

groups.name: Where it is
text: The street and city are optional; the country is not.
The coordinates are never typed in. They come from *geocoding* the address: looking up where that address is on a map.

address_line1.means: The street address, when one was given. It can be empty.

city.means: The town or city, when one was given.

country_code.means: The country, as a two-letter code from the ISO 3166-1 standard, always in capitals. Required, even when there is no address.

examples.GB: the United Kingdom: the standard says `GB`, not `UK`

latitude.means: How far north (positive) or south (negative) of the equator the venue is, in degrees. The type `numeric(9,6)` is an exact decimal with up to 9 digits, 6 of them after the point, which pins a spot to about 10 cm. Set by geocoding the address, not typed in.

longitude.means: How far east (positive) or west (negative) of Greenwich the venue is, in degrees, in the same `numeric(9,6)` form. Also set by geocoding the address.

records.name: Everything filled in
records.text: Harbour Hall has an address, coordinates and a capacity. Its two zones, Floor and Balcony, are rows in [[seating_zones]].

records.name: A venue abroad

records.name: Only what is required
records.text: Saved with just a name, a country and a time zone. There is no address, so no coordinates either, and nobody has filled in the capacity.

scenarios.title: Someone tries to delete a venue that still has events
text: Lakeside Pavilion hosted Lakeside Acoustic Night, which was cancelled. Cancelling keeps the event's row, and its `venue_id` on [[events]] still points here.
That link refuses the delete, so the venue stays for as long as any event, cancelled or not, points at it.

scenarios.title: A venue no event uses is deleted
scenarios.text: No event points at Pop-up space, so nothing refuses the delete. The row goes, and any [[seating_zones]] it had go with it.

scenarios.title: The organization is deleted
scenarios.text: Deleting an organization deletes its venues and their seating zones. It is refused, though, while the organization still has events, orders, payments or payout batches, and in practice organizations are soft-deleted instead.

waitlist_entries.purpose: One row per person waiting for a ticket that is sold out.

columns.ticket_type_id: NULL to wait for any ticket type, or cleared when that type is deleted
columns.user_id: NULL when someone joined the waitlist without signing in
columns.email: One entry per email per event
columns.expires_at: When an offer lapses and the stock goes to the next person

notes: The release job walks `status = 'waiting'` in `created_at` order, oldest first.

examples.intro: A waitlist entry is one person queuing for tickets that are sold out. When stock comes free, the oldest waiting entry gets an offer, which holds the stock until it expires.

groups.name: Who is waiting, and for what
groups.text: One entry per email per event: the same address can't queue twice for the same event.

id.means: The internal number of the entry.

event_id.means: The event they are waiting for. Deleting the event deletes its waitlist.

ticket_type_id.means: The ticket type they want, from [[ticket_types]]. NULL means any ticket type will do; it is also cleared if that type is deleted.

user_id.means: The signed-in person, when there is one. NULL when someone joined without signing in, and cleared if their account is deleted.

email.means: The person's email. Required even when `user_id` is set, and unique per event.

quantity_wanted.means: How many tickets they want, from 1 to 10; the database checks the range. It is 1 unless they ask for more.

scenarios.title: The same email joins twice
scenarios.text: Chen is already on the waitlist for event 3064 and tries to join it again with the same email. The second entry is refused.

groups.name: Where it is in the queue
text: The waitlist release job runs every five minutes. When stock comes free, it offers it to the oldest `waiting` entry for the event, oldest by `created_at`, and queues a notification.

An offer holds the stock until `expires_at`. If it isn't taken by then, the entry becomes `expired` and the stock moves to the next `waiting` entry. The table shows the queue for event 3064, oldest first.

status.means: Where the entry is right now.

examples.waiting: In the queue. Every entry starts here.
examples.offered: Freed stock is being held for this person until `expires_at`.
examples.expired: The offer wasn't taken before `expires_at`; the stock moved on to the next person.

offered_at.means: When the release job made the offer. Empty while the entry is still `waiting`.

expires_at.means: When the offer lapses and the stock goes to the next person. Set with the offer, so empty while the entry is still `waiting`.

created_at.means: When the person joined. The release job serves entries oldest first by this time.

webhook_deliveries.purpose: One row per webhook the platform tried to deliver to an organizer's endpoint.

columns.event_name: Which platform event this payload describes
columns.target_url: Copied from the endpoint's settings at send time, so the history stays true
columns.payload: Exactly what was sent, including the signature header's body
columns.attempt_count: Retries back off; the sender gives up after 8
columns.response_code: HTTP status of the last attempt. NULL if the request never completed

notes: Rows older than 30 days are deleted by the nightly job.

examples.intro: A *webhook* is a web request the platform sends to an organizer's own system to tell it that something happened, such as an order being paid. Each row is one such message, with every attempt to deliver it counted on the same row.

groups.name: Whose webhook, and when
groups.text: Rows older than 30 days are deleted by the nightly purge, so this table only holds the last month or so.

id.means: The internal number, for joins only.

organization_id.means: The organizer whose endpoint the webhook was sent to. If the organization row is deleted, its deliveries go with it.

created_at.means: When the delivery was created, before the first attempt.

groups.name: What was sent
groups.text: *Event* here means something that happened on the platform, not a row in [[events]]: an order being paid is an event in this sense too.

event_name.means: Which platform event the payload describes.

examples.order.refunded: Money went back on an order.
examples.attendee.checked_in: A ticket was checked in at the door.

payload.means: Exactly what was sent, including the signature header's body. A *signature* lets the receiver check that the request really came from the platform. The column is *jsonb*: JSON that PostgreSQL stores already parsed, so it can be searched by key.

target_url.means: The organizer's *endpoint*: the web address their system receives webhooks at. Copied from the endpoint's settings at send time, so the history stays true even if the organizer changes the address later.

scenarios.title: The organizer changes their endpoint
scenarios.text: Organization 12 later moves its endpoint to a new address. Rows already sent keep the address they really went to; only new rows get the new one.

groups.name: Did it get there
text: A delivery that fails is tried again by the retry worker, waiting longer between tries each time (*backing off*).
The sender gives up after 8 attempts. The retry worker's queue is the `failed` rows with fewer than 8.

status.means: Whether the webhook got through. A new row starts as `pending`, the column's default.

examples.failed: The last attempt failed. With fewer than 8 attempts the retry worker tries again; at 8 the sender has given up.

attempt_count.means: How many times delivery has been tried. Starts at `0` and can never go below it.

response_code.means: The *HTTP status code* the endpoint answered the last attempt with: the three-digit number every web server sends back. NULL if the request never completed, for example when the address could not be reached.
examples: the organizer's server hit an error

last_attempt_at.means: When delivery was last tried. Empty until the first attempt. The retry worker goes by this time.

records.name: Delivered first time
records.text: Organization 12's system hears that Amira's order 90412 was paid. The endpoint answers `200` on the first try.

records.name: Failing, still retried
records.text: Three tries so far, and the last one got `503`: the organizer's server was unavailable. With fewer than 8 attempts, the row is still in the retry worker's queue.

records.name: Given up
records.text: Eight attempts, and no answer to the last one, so `response_code` is empty. The sender has stopped trying.

records.name: Not tried yet
records.text: Just created when event 3112 was cancelled. No attempt yet, so the attempt columns are still at their starting values.

scenarios.title: The organizer's server is down for a while
text: Organization 27's server is down when an event is published. The first attempt gets `503`, and the row becomes `failed`.
The retry worker tries again, waiting longer each time. The fourth attempt gets `200`, and the row is `delivered`.

scenarios.title: A month later
scenarios.text: Once a row is more than 30 days old, the nightly purge deletes it, whatever its status.

tour.title: The database in one sentence
text: One PostgreSQL database runs the whole ticketing platform: **{tables} tables**, grouped into **{areas} areas**.
Read it as a shop. An organizer lists an event, a buyer fills a basket, money moves, and someone scans a barcode at the door.

tour.title: Everything belongs to an organization
text: `organizations` is the tenant. {in:organizations} links from {inFrom:organizations} tables point to it, more than to any other table.
`org_members` says who may act for one. It has no id of its own: the pair of organization and user *is* the key, so one person holds one role per organization.

tour.title: An organization can own another one
text: `organizations.parent_org_id` points back at `organizations`. A venue group uses it for its sub-accounts, which share billing.
Delete a parent and the children stay, with `parent_org_id` cleared. Nothing cascades.

tour.title: Where an event happens
text: A venue belongs to one organization. `seating_zones` splits the room into named parts, which reserved ticket types point at.
Deleting a venue is refused while any event still points at it. Deleting the organization takes its venues with it.

tour.title: An event's life
text: `events.status` is the one column that decides whether the public can see the event and whether tickets can be bought.
`cancelled` can be reached from any step, and is never a delete: the row has to survive so its tickets and payments still make sense.

tour.title: What an event sells
text: `ticket_types` is the thing a buyer actually puts in a basket: a name, a price and a quantity. `event_sessions` only exists for events that run more than once.
`discount_codes` can hang off one event or off the whole organization.

tour.title: A basket becomes an order
text: A basket is a real `orders` row from the first ticket added, so held stock is visible to everyone. `status = 'cart'` keeps it out of every report.
`order_lines` has a composite primary key: `(order_id, line_no)`. Line numbers start at 1 inside an order and are never reused.

tour.title: One row per ticket, with a name on it
text: Buying three tickets on one line creates three `attendees` rows. That is where the barcode lives, and the only id the door app ever sees.
`attendees` points at `order_lines` with **two** columns at once, because the line it came from needs both.

tour.title: What happens when something is deleted
text: Every link says what happens to a row when the row it points at is deleted. There are three answers, and the schema uses all three.

visual.cascade: An event's ticket types, sessions and attendees go with it. {cascade} links work this way.
visual.setnull: A deleted staff account leaves its check-ins in place with `checked_in_by` empty. {setnull} links.
visual.restrict: An order with a payment against it refuses to be deleted. {restrict} links.

tour.title: Money in, money out
text: `payments` is one row per *attempt*, so a failed card is a row too. At most one of them succeeded.
`refunds` can be partial and can be several per payment. `payout_batches` sweeps succeeded payments into one transfer to the organizer.

tour.title: At the door, and in the queue
text: `check_ins` records every scan, including the ones turned away, so a disputed night can be read back. A unique index allows only one `ok` scan per ticket.
`waitlist_entries` is the queue for a sold-out type. An offer holds stock until it expires, then moves to the next person.

tour.title: Where to go next
text: `notifications`, `webhook_deliveries` and `audit_log` are the platform's own record of what it sent and who changed what. None of them is read by the app itself.
Explore walks the areas table by table. Reference has every link, every index and every rule in one list.

reference.title: Conventions
reference.desc: The patterns nearly every table follows

items.title: Internal keys
items.text: `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`. For joins only, and **never sent to a client**.

items.title: Public keys
items.text: `public_id uuid` on every row a client can name, so nothing can be guessed or counted from a URL.

items.title: Slugs
items.text: `organizations.slug` and `events.slug` name those rows in public URLs. Event slugs are unique inside the organization, not globally.

items.title: Money
items.text: Integer cents plus a `char(3)` currency on the same row. No floats anywhere, and no implied currency.

items.title: Timestamps
items.text: `timestamptz`, always absolute. `events.timezone` and `venues.timezone` say how to show them. `updated_at` is set by the application, not by a trigger.

items.title: Status columns
items.text: `text` with `CHECK (… IN (…))`, so the database rejects an unknown value. The same lists are generated into `app/types/status.ts` by `rake schema:types`.

items.title: Soft delete
items.text: `deleted_at` on `organizations` and `users` only. Everything else is deleted for real or cancelled in place.

items.title: Stored counts
items.text: `ticket_types.quantity_sold` and `discount_codes.redemption_count` are moved inside the checkout transaction and repaired nightly. A CHECK stops `quantity_sold` passing `quantity_total`.

items.title: Denormalised ids
items.text: `attendees.event_id`, `check_ins.event_id` and `refunds.order_id` repeat an id that could be joined for. They exist so the door app and the finance reports stay on one table.

items.title: Ordered children
items.text: `position` on `event_sessions`, `seating_zones` and `ticket_types`. Renumbered from 0 on every save, in one statement.

items.title: Polymorphic references
items.text: `audit_log.entity_type` and `audit_log.entity_id` have no foreign key on purpose, so the log outlives the rows it describes.

items.title: Cents, not currency maths
items.text: Totals are checked by the database: `orders.total_cents` against its three parts, `order_lines.line_total_cents` against unit price and quantity, `payout_batches.net_cents` against gross and fees.

reference.title: How data changes and expires
reference.desc: Status flows, the jobs that move them, and what is cleaned up

items.title: An event
items.text: `cancelled` is reachable from any step. `sold_out` is set by the checkout job when the last ticket type fills, and back to `on_sale` when a refund frees stock.

items.title: An order
items.text: Then `partially_refunded` or `refunded` as money goes back. `cancelled` is for an organizer cancelling, `expired` for the basket sweeper.

items.title: A ticket
items.text: `transferred` means the name changed. `void` is set by a full refund or by a fraud case, and a void ticket is refused at the door.

items.title: A waitlist entry
items.text: `expired` when an offer is not taken before `expires_at`. The stock then moves to the next `waiting` row.

sections.title: Jobs that write to the database

items.title: Basket sweeper
items.text: Hourly. Sets `orders.status = 'expired'` past `expires_at` and lowers `ticket_types.quantity_sold` by what the basket held.

items.title: Waitlist release
items.text: Every five minutes. Offers freed stock to the oldest `waiting` entry and queues a notification.

items.title: Payout sweep
items.text: Weekly. Opens a `payout_batches` row per organization and sets `payments.payout_batch_id` on the succeeded payments inside the period.

items.title: Count repair
items.text: Nightly. Recounts `ticket_types.quantity_sold` and `discount_codes.redemption_count` from the orders and corrects any drift.

items.title: Purge
items.text: Nightly. Removes `organizations` and `users` rows soft-deleted more than 30 days ago, `webhook_deliveries` older than 30 days, and `user_devices` unused for 90 days.

sections.title: What survives a delete
sections.note: Deleting a `users` row clears `orders.user_id` but keeps the order, its lines, its attendees and its payments. The buyer's email stays on the order, because a guest order has nothing else to find it by.

items.title: Deleting an organization
items.text: Refused while it has events, orders, payments or payout batches. In practice organizations are soft-deleted instead.

items.title: Deleting an event
items.text: Takes its sessions, ticket types, discount codes, attendees, check-ins and waitlist with it. Refused while it has orders.

items.title: Deleting an order
items.text: Takes its lines and their attendees and check-ins. Refused while a payment or refund points at it.
